# Copper October 2010 

- On the final two trading days of September, copper prices easily surged past their target level for the month ($8000/t). Since then quotes for the red metal have remained comfortably above that point for all of October.  However, after hitting the next target of $8500/t on October 25th, there are some signs that copper could ease back in the very short term. 

- After extensive discussions during LME Week with several copper users, we have raised our 2010 estimated and 2011 forecast copper consumption figures by 435kt and 285kt, respectively, leaving global demand for this year up by almost a full 10% on last year at 19.227Mt.  Somewhat surprisingly, the focus of this improvement has been outside China; indeed, the unexpected weakness currently being experienced in Chinese copper markets may in fact force us to revise down that country’s demand estimate for this year in subsequent reports (see below).  Over 140kt of this increase for this year has been allocated to Western Europe, 50-60kt each to Japan and Asia, and a further 120kt or so into Eastern Europe, including Russia. 

- One hot topic of discussion during LME Week was the establishment of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for base metals, and even before the month was out, two companies had filed applications with the US Securities and Exchange Commission for such a purpose - JP Morgan and Blackrock Asset Management - with at least two others (ETF Securities and Credit Suisse) far down the planning road for their own ETF. 

- The marked change in sentiment in the copper concentrates market last month that led to a significant rise in spot terms showed little sign of abating during October.  Although the rate of increase slowed somewhat, most observers believe that TC/RCs will move yet higher before topping out.  One consequence of rising spot rates is that many deals are now being transacted outside of the normal tendering process and we hear that prompt sales between mines and traders have recently realised terms of between $75-80/t & 7.5-8.0c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Copper prices nudge past $8500/t mark** On the final two trading days of Septemb

er, copper prices easily surged past their target level for the month ($8000/t).  Since then quotes for the red metal have remained comfortably above that point for all of October.  However, after hitting the next target of $8500/t on October 25<sup>th</sup> , there are some signs that copper could ease back in the very short term, despite the potential for what would be a price-supportive strike at the Collahuasi mine in Chile which could begin as early as November 5<sup>th</sup> .  Overriding this issue is the lack of direction from the financial sector as it awaits early November clarification from the US Federal Reserve regarding the extent of its next quantitative easing decisions. 

**Encouraging economic data lays the basis for bullish LME Week** Despite the odd pause for breath, copper prices rushed headlong into a virtual two-week bull run from the opening trading day of this month all the way through to LME Week.  In a way, it was not surprising that the traditional autumn industry gathering saw higher prices, given that the general mood was far better than that of a year ago, and a dissenting bearish voice was rarely heard.  Even prior to LME Week, though, generally improving global economic data sets were supportive of base metal demand figures.  Indeed, conversations we held with metal users during LME Week have convinced us that metals demand across the board has been even stronger than we have previously considered, including in copper, and we have reflected this sentiment with extensive upgrades to demand this year and into 2011. 

**Dollar drives copper forward in October** Sentiment aside, although global financial markets are without clear direction as we head into the first week of November, the dollar has once again been the main force behind metal price movements during much of this month, and arguably even before.  Monetary policy in the US has been driving financial markets to a high degree of late, ever since some hints on August 27<sup>th</sup> from US Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke that quantitative easing (QE) may be re-started.  Although no announcement has yet been made about QE2 in the US, markets have become increasingly certain that it will occur.  This could turn out to be a double bonus for metals prices, as first of all it has pushed down the value of the dollar (by ~5% on a trade weighted basis), boosting metal prices.  In addition, QE can change the balance of risks in the market, pushing investors out of government bonds and into riskier assets such as equities and commodities. 

However, in the final week of October US macro data has been decidedly mixed and there is thus an equally mixed opinion over whether QE2 will come in one large, single package, or whether it will be drip-fed into the economy.  With the potential of too much QE having been priced in too soon, the slide on the dollar and the rally in metals and equities ground to a halt on the 26<sup>th</sup> , and copper prices fell back from

their $8500/t seven-month high (cash) to $8466 on the 26th , and then to $8332/t a day later. From here, all eyes will be on the Fed’s meeting on November 2nd and 3rd . #### **Copper price and $US trade-weighted index** 9,000 90

**Copper demand still strong into November, but little clarity into Q1** A second factor in the price slide during the final week of October has been a general consensus that physical buying will begin to tail off for the rest of the year as the December holiday season approaches. Several copper suppliers said to us this month that November’s orders have remained strong, but beyond that they will be subject to the usual seasonality and widespread practice of reducing inventory as much as possible. Although there was general optimism for 2011 as a whole, there is little in the way of clarity on likely first quarter orders at this stage. **Stocks, premia, generally supportive of prices** Meanwhile, the usual market parameters this month have been generally supportive of bullish prices. After ending September on 373.8kt, LME copper stocks fell slightly to 368kt on the 28th of this month (the 26th actually recorded the recent low of 367.5kt). Equally, Comex saw its stock levels fall on a gradual basis from end September’s 77kt to 68.5kt on October 28th . However, these combined reductions were more than offset by a rise in Chinese exchange stocks, where ample cathode supplies have come up against surprisingly weak markets. Consequently, cathode stocks on the SHFE rose from 87.4kt at the start of this month to 106.3kt on the 22nd , and premia in China slipped by $10/t to $115/t. Since then, we have heard of premia falling even further, to below $80/t, as sudden softness hit the Chinese market, which is somewhat surprising given that this should be a strong month (even with the holidays taken into account) ahead of seasonal domestic and export demand. Premia in Europe and the US have maintained September’s levels, with only Singapore showing any softening month on month. **Codelco sets its 201

1 European premia at $98/t** Reflecting its opinion of copper demand in Europe next year, Codelco this month set its contract premium for Grade A cathode at $98/t. This is 22.5% up on last year’s level of US$80/t, and considerably above even the highest spot premia of $90-95/t currently. Although this is still below the recent records of $125/t in 2007 and $115/t in 2008, it is a measure of the strength in some existing markets and an indication of anticipated tightness in quality cathode regionally. While some consumers do not share that “tightness” view, the anticipated increase in Russia’s refined copper export duty (from 0% to 10%) next year will dramatically increase rod exports at the expense of cathodes which will lend support to Codelco’s outlook (see Consumption section). #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 Refined Imports 400

**ETF’s prove to be main talking point during LME Week** One hot topic of discussion during LME Week was the establishment of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) backed by physical base metals, and even before the month was out, two companies had filed applications with the US Securities and Exchange Commission for such a purpose - JP Morgan and Blackrock Asset Management - with at least two others (ETF Securities and Credit Suisse) far down the planning road for their own ETF. The desire by investors to gain direct exposure to the price performance of hard assets such as physical base metals has never been stronger. The same is, of course, true of asset managers and their brokers in terms of their desire to develop new investment vehicles along with their associated fee structures. Unlike the futures and options markets, participating in metal ownership is not time limited and the costs of rolling positions and/or covering potentially large margin calls are also removed. In addition, participating in metal ownership has the added benefit over indirect participation via the equities markets as it circumvents issues outside of the control of the investor such as company performance risk and dividend policy. The proposed mechanism for these ETFs involves would-be investors accessing the physical metal markets through buying units in a dedicated fun

d that acts as the custodian of metal/metal warrants. While much of the desire to own hard assets arises within the investment community, some producers, most notably in aluminium, are also keen to establish ETFs as another mechanism for tying up unsold metal inventories. 

Although the concept of a physical base metal ETF has yet to be tested, ETFs have operated successfully within the precious metals sector since 2003.  This is because the supply/demand characteristics of a metal such as gold, with its limited industrial consumption base and historic function as bullion mean that physically-backed hoarding of gold for investment purposes presents very few issues for this market.  Indeed, SPDR Gold Trust fund is now the world’s sixthlargest holder of physical gold.  However, the same may not be true for industrial metals, especially under tight market conditions.  A concern is that metal held in an ETF would be yet another way of depriving the industrial sector of liquid stock resulting in spot metal premia rising far higher than would normally be the case.  Moreover, a significant supply disruption is likely to fuel ETF buying, thereby exacerbating the situation. 

The outcome of an ETF on the market will depend on how it operates.  If it were set up "off-exchange", like JP Morgan intends to do, then a scenario of elevated premia and price under tight market conditions is likely to occur as stock movements will be opaque to the market and lend the impression of real metal consumption rather than stock merely moving into a warehouse or from one warehouse to another.  An "on-exchange" ETF is likely to firm up premia and not necessarily prices _per se_ , given that each stock movement will be visible to the market.  This latter mechanism, currently proposed by both Blackrock and ETF Securities, may be more appealing to investors than an off-exchange fund, given the increased level of regulatory protection in a market that would also be backed by highly liquid metal warrants. However, the custodian of warrants that are held on-exchange would come under the same LME rules and regulations as any other participant as regards lending guidance, including the requirement for dominant position holders to lend metal under certain market conditions.  A fund might thus be forced to reduce its positions, leaving it without control over its inventories which would mean that the product would no longer be properly backed by physical metal.  While an ETF fund operating in markets that have large exchange inventories, such as aluminium and zinc, is unlikely to reach dominant position holder status, this may not be the case for copper or tin where overall inventories are far lower. 

The costs associated with a base metal ETF will be higher in percentage terms than for precious metals.  This is because warehousing and insurance costs per tonne of the latter are much lower as an overall percentage of the value of these commodities.  Also if the metal held under an

on-exchange ETF were to be located in the same country as the

jurisdiction under which the ETF is operated, this would by preference be in a single warehouse or in a select number of warehouses to minimise unit storage costs.  In order to achieve this, warrants would need to be "sifted" or purchased directly from a producer but either way, these would include the prevailing seller's premia to LME prices which would also add to overall costs. 

Ultimately, for an ETF to be successfully subscribed to there must be the belief amongst investors that prices will trade higher.  ScotiaMocatta failed on two occasions to establish a physical copper fund, firstly in late 2009 and then again in April 2010, because it was unable to raise the necessary C$100M required to meet the fund's minimum threshold. However, market sentiment has moved on and at present, the general consensus is that copper's robust fundamentals should result in higher prices in the short to medium term, making it the most desirable metal for an ETF.  Currently, both JP Morgan’s and Blackrock’s ETF plans are to be backed by copper alone, while ETF Securities intends to start ETF’s across six base metals and Credit Suisse is looking at aluminium.  For a metal such as aluminium, which is currently in profound structural oversupply and where the price outlook is less optimistic, an ETF product is unlikely to be as appealing to the retail sector, but it may attract investors with longer term objectives. 

The real risk to copper is that by exposing the physical metal market to further widespread speculation this can only add a new dimension of price volatility while also potentially disrupting the main purpose of these markets which is to ensure the orderly buying and selling of metals for industrial purposes.  Copper's main challenge may be the impact of artificially high prices on demand destruction and on accelerating the pace of substitution.  Chinese consumers are already attempting to engineer copper out of any manufactured product where possible.  Also, the combination of highly volatile copper prices and spot premia is problematic for all consumers in terms of their financing, credit cover and insurance requirements.  Ultimately, though, we go back to whether or not there will be enough high net-worth individuals that are prepared to ensure the viability of and need for this new investment risk vehicle.  As one copper distributor said to us “we’re at a time when the clever money is getting out, and the stupid money is staying in”.  If so, then only time will tell how much “stupid money” there is to go around. 

**Price forecasts move higher for the next two years** Given that one of the key criteria for a physical metal ETF to succeed is higher short- to medium-term prices (backed either by a real or perceived market shortage), then our current outlook indeed suggests that an ETF will do

well. Our revisions this month, based on extensive discussion with the industry, have given rise to a deficit this year of 266kt, followed by a near 0.5Mt metal shortfall next year. Consequently, with our metal stock days of consumption falling below 60 for this year and to well below 50 for 2011 and 2012, our price projections have moved up quite dramatically to average almost $4.00/lb for the next two years. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

Somewhat surprisingly, the focus of this improvement has been outside China; indeed, the unexpected weakness currently being experienced in Chinese copper markets may in fact force us to revise down that country’s demand estimate for this year in subsequent reports (see below). Over 140kt of this increase for this year has been allocated to Western Europe, 50-60kt each to Japan and Asia, and a further 120kt or so into Eastern Europe, including Russia. ### **Europe and CIS** **Regional copper demand increased to 3.94Mt** We have increased our forecast of copper demand for the region this year from 3.61Mt to 3.94Mt since our September report, given the stronger first eight months of the year than previously anticipated. Germany, Belgium, Italy, Poland and Russia account for the lion’s share of the improvement, where many rod mills have managed to increase their capacity utilisation rate this year to c.75% from 60-65%. A

lthough the rod for railways demand segment has yet to recover because of deferred projects, enamelled wire markets for winding wire and motors, especially for the automotive sector, have recovered well.  The one clause here though is that in many cases, such as Germany, the resurging automotive market has come from export demand, with Asia leading the way, as domestic sales continue to be flat following the end of the scrapping subsidy schemes.  Overall, vehicle assemblies in Western Europe have exceeded expectations, and are in distinct contrast to what has been going on with domestic sales.  Germany is perhaps the prime example of this.  In July, year on year auto production went negative, but strengthened in August and September, leaving year to date figures up by 18%.  Sales, on the other hand continue to contract, and are down by 25% year on year to September. 

For Western Europe as a whole, output is expected to rise by 9% this year, with particularly strong growth in the UK and Sweden.  The impending austerity measures looming for many Euro nations will act as a constraint on demand and production in 2011, and signs of slowing production are already in evidence.  Total production growth for 2011 is forecast at an anaemic 0.6%. 

**Construction remains poorest segment in Europe** In copper tube markets, this year has seen a recovery from last year, although clearly not back to pre-crisis levels.  Some markets (automotive, electronics) are doing well, but construction markets remain low because of poor new build rates, and some sanitary tubing has already moved across to plastics because of copper’s relatively high price.  Equally, the roofing sector is fragile because of price sensitivity. Euro zone construction output fell a further 0.4% mom and 8.5% year on year in August, led by a slump in Spain, Germany and Holland.  In contrast, strong gains were recorded in the UK and some Eastern economies such as Poland. Civil engineering has been particularly weak, and will likely continue to be so due to all the cutbacks. 

While still dreary, there were a few rays of light in EU construction indicators.  Although new orders and total activity are still in contraction territory on the PMIs, housing activity moved above the 50 threshold in September for the first time since April 2007, and commercial activity was 49.4, the highest value since May 2008.  The data suggest that perhaps some increased investment should be expected in early 2011.  Even so, EU industry faces some heavy headwinds for early 2011.  Austerity measures are likely to act as a constraint on domestic demand, and there is only small scope for growth from abroad.  The only silver lining here is possibly the euro, which we expect to weaken further next year, boosting the competitiveness of EU manufacturing. 

**Q4 looking strong, equally so 2011** All of the European copper processors we spoke with during LME Week expressed surprise at the strength of their order books, though, f

or this final quarter of the year. Equally, they are optimistic for 2011, although many expressed little long-term visibility. As per last year, this year’s contract sales have included a “flexibility” clause in which buyers can take at their option an additional percentage of material at the contract price terms, rather than at spot market rates. Consequently, this lends optimism to total sales for next year, but leaves considerable margin for uncertainty. Also, the “additional” material that can be bought under contract terms would have been referred to as “spot” business in pre-crisis conditions, and yet it will probably be referred to as “contract” if this portion is indeed taken up. This traditional distinction between spot and contract will continue to be blurred into 2011 as it has in 2010, and will create the impression that there is no spot business when in reality there is, and has been this year. **Russia likely to cut cathode exports, boost rod in 2011** With the Russian government likely to impose a 10% export tax on copper cathode exports from next January, we anticipate a similar shift in product trade that we have seen before in which domestic producers retain cathode at home and instead convert it into wire rod for the export market in order to avoid the tax. This will, according to one European wire rod producer, be the single largest influence on sport cathode premia going forward. Currently, there is sufficient cathode in the European market, but the removal of, say, 300-400kt Russian cathode will push the cathode balance into a small deficit. However, we are not anticipating such a wholesale shift in product trade patterns as last time because one Russian cathode producer, Uralelectromed’s Pyshma refinery, gained LME product certification in July, thereby allowing Pyshma’s cathodes to obtain higher sales prices which could be sufficient to offset the export tax. Although IP and capacity utilisation have continued to improve, the pace has slowed. Production of electrical equipment is constrained by the weakness in construction, and the slowdown in recovery in the autos markets is also having a noticeable effect. The headline and new order PMIs remain above the 50 threshold for expansion, but have both fallen significantly and are now at 2010 lows. We expect IP to be virtually unchanged from September levels for 4Q10 and 1Q11, with modest recovery beginning in Q2, when underlying consumption starts to improve. #### **US copper wire rod production – (kt)** 40 125

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - October 2010 Page 7 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **US ITC confirms tube import anti-dumping duties** US copper and copper alloy semis shipments of 581.5kt (metric) for January to July this year was up by 13.7% on the same period last year. While this reflects improved demand levels, the introduction of an anti-dumping duty on copper tube imports from both Mexico and China has had a measurable impact and forced US consumers to turn to domestically-made goods. Imports of pure copper tube were down from 61.3kt (short) for the January-July 2009 period to 49.1kt (short) this year. Last month we reported on the trade case against certain Chinese and Mexican exports of copper tube products into the USA, and that the International Trade Commission had issued a ruling which effectively imposed preliminary heavy tariffs on the companies cited (see September’s report). On October 26th , the ITC issued its final determination which agreed with its earlier findings, and now anti-dumping orders can legally be applied to all the companies named in the case. This should have the effect of reducing still further such imports of tube, leaving the US manufacturers to continue their recovery. ### **China** **The growth of China's industrial value-added output grew by 13.3% in September** China’s industrial production grew by 13.3% year on year in September, the fourth consecutive month that growth has been between 13 and 14%. It would seem that cooling measures have been successful in bringing growth down to more stable levels, as reflected in our reduced forecast for 2011 growth of 12.9%. The reason behind the WM forecast cut was primarily reduced investment in construction (excluding infrastructure) following this year’s policy tightening. However, there have been indications in the past week that further cuts may be needed. Recent government meetings in Beijing around the next five-year plan

have resulted in a change in policy rhetoric. The idea of supporting GDP growth of at least 8% p.a. irrespective of the consequences seems to have been abandoned. The previous, almost “guarantee” of 8% growth essentially meant that capital investment would always generate a good return, and hence spurred over-investment. Instead, the focus has been shifted to growth in consumption, boosting household income and reducing exports. To show this is not mere words, interest rates were unexpectedly increased on October 19th for the first time in three years, and bank reserve requirements rose. Structural change will be slow in coming, but the rate at which China’s economy becomes less industry-, and hence metal-intensive, should now be accelerated. **Shanghai copper trades lower than the LME** The copper price in Shanghai’s physical market was US$330/t lower than the LME+tax and import cost for most of the time in October, reflecting higher cathode supplies in China and weak demand from the fabricators. In general, cathode demand this month has been quite weak even though October should be a traditionally strong month. Having the one-week’s holiday kept business low; furthermore, the generally higher copper price has encouraged higher scrap usage by the fabricators. Copper semis output for September dipped to a sixmonth low of 842.4kt, down from the prior month’s 862.1kt. Even so, this still leaves year on year production up by 14.8%, at 7.255Mt. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1000

**Government-driven energy and emissions cuts keep lid on growth** The slowdown in industrial production growth and economic expansion was a result of government macro-control measures. Local governments in China had taken great steps to cut energy consumption and reduce emissions this year, which largely curbed the growth of high energyconsuming industries. The growth of China's heavy industries was also expected to further decelerate over the coming months as China will continue to work to conserve energy and cut emissions. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - October 2010 Page 8 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Power cuts expanded to other provinces** Some fabricators, including one big sheet/strip makers and wire rod maker in Anhui province, complained that their electricity supply was limited in October, and this has been one reason for lower copper products output and demand this month. Order books at some major copper sheet/strip makers in October were down by around 20% from September. Normally October is the high season for Christmas orders, but we have not seen this usual peak this year. Both connector and lead frame makers reduced their orders due to th

eir high inventories, reflecting the high inventories in electronic industry and home electrical appliances. **Demand for wire rod is still weak** Meanwhile, order books at some major wire rod makers in October fell by 20-30% from the peak in the first half of this year. Slow growth rates of home electrical appliances and auto production are the main reasons. Although copper demand from the power cable sector recovered a little from August and July following additional investment in the power grid in September, it is still weak. High copper prices have initiated some substitution of copper by aluminium in the wire and cable industry. Consequently, we might not see a pick-up in wire rod demand for the rest of this year, and so for this month we have left Chinese copper demand unchanged for 2010 at 7.368Mt. According to the latest data issued by China Electricity Council, investment in the power industry during the first nine months of the year increased by 2.2% year on year. Investment in power generation increased by 15% year on year, which has mainly gone to some new energy projects. Copper Monthly Update 

**Chinese market remains highly unpredictable with record concentrate imports in September** The highly unpredictable nature of the Chinese market has been brought to the fore once again in September.  Last month we reported that the country’s imports of copper concentrates had been on a declining year-on-year trend since May.  We also highlighted the fact that Chinese buyers had all but withdrawn from the international spot market which was one of the key reasons for the significant uplift in spot terms.  With these points in mind, the latest official customs statistics show that China’s copper concentrates imports during September reached an all-time high of 683.5kdmt which was not only up by 21.6% on the same month last year but also 27.5kt higher than the previous monthly record established in June 2009.  Following this strong performance, year to date imports have surged to 4.96Mdmt or 6% above what was achieved in the January through September period in 2009.  Chile remains the largest supplier with a market share of 28% followed by Peru (14%), Australia (9%) and

Mongolia (8%). 

**More reasons emerge as to why China has exited the spot market** The very high level of concentrate imports during September goes part way to explaining China’s recent actions in terms of backing away from the spot market.  However, our discussions during LME Week revealed other factors that have contributed to this situation.  Perhaps the most significant relates to Chinese domestic mine production which has increased quite markedly this year.  This has resulted to some extent from the reactivation of mines that were closed in Q1 2009 on account of low prices.  Also, a number of new operations have been commissioned over the past year, most notably in Inner Mongolia.  This is reflected in official data with China’s copper-in-concentrates production having risen by 21% year on year, or by 142kt Cu to 821kt Cu in the 9m period to September 2010 with 62kt of this emanating from Inner Mongolia, 31kt from Yunnan province and 15kt from Xinjiang province.  Estimates of total Chinese copper-in-concentrates production for this year range from 1.1Mt to 1.2Mt (our number is 1.15Mt) which is almost 20% above the 962kt produced in 2009.  There has also been a rise in output from Chinese smelters that have no associated refinery (Fangtai, Liangshan and Hengbang) with blister/anode from these plants having been sold to domestic refiners.  In addition, imports of blister copper have been running almost 125kt above last year’s nine-month level which has also dampened demand for imported concentrates.  Chinese authorities also introduced new environmental emissions standards in May 2010 that have forced a number of smelters to reduce output in order to meet these more stringent targets.  Seemingly, smelters are given up to 3 warnings for exceeding new emission limits before their power supply is simply cut off!  Some smelters have also been affected by power rationing particularly in the country’s eastern provinces.  A number of smelters have encountered operational problems of late including Baiyin, Yantai and Zhongtiaoshan which has led to a redistribution of concentrates to other smelters.  Also, as we have mentioned previously, the Chinese smelting and refining sectors have had more access to scrap than their manufacturing counterparts due to better credit availability.  Finally, an unfavourable copper price arbitrage between the SHFE and the LME has further dampened demand for overseas concentrates.  The culmination of all of these points is that presently many Chinese smelters have ample stocks of concentrates and this is perhaps the main factor as to why some market commentators believe that the world’s largest buyer of custom copper concentrates may not return to the spot market until perhaps after the Chinese New Year. 

**Mating Season negotiations get off to a quiet start** Although the concentrate Mating Season officially kicked off during October, unusually there has been very little progress to report.  This may be due to BHP Bil

liton’s apparent strategy this year of not entering into any heavyweight first round meetings during LME Week.  We hear that the company’s initial negotiations with its Japanese counterparts are due to start in Hong Kong towards the end of this month.  While most of the major players are, as expected playing their cards close to their chests, China’s CSPT has made it known that its TC/RC objective for the 2011 Mating Season is $75/t & 7.5c/lb.  While these terms are some $10/t & 1c/lb below current Chinese spot rates they are considerably above last year’s long-term benchmark of $46.5/t & 4.65c/lb.  One of the key questions is whether current spot rates are indicative of the market moving forward?  According to our analysis and as highlighted in last month’s report, we estimate that copper-in-concentrate supplies next year will satisfy around 80% of overall primary smelter capacity, which is similar to this year.  Ideally, the primary smelting industry should operate at an optimal level of 88% of capacity and, if mine supplies exceed this rate then concentrate stocks tend to accumulate within the system as was last seen in 2004 and 2005 when global copper-in-concentrate production was equivalent to 94% and 90% of primary smelter capacity respectively.  Under current market conditions it is clear that many smelters are operating at subpar levels for example in Japan, where PPC and SMM are running their plants well below normal levels (13% and 10% respectively).  Elsewhere, both Indian smelters are producing less than their optimal rates for one reason or another.  On the basis that overall primary smelter operating rates remain at 80% next year due to mine supply constraints then in overall tonnage terms, this will leave primary smelters short of around 1.4Mt relative to optimal rates.  This implies that various smelter production cuts will have to remain in place and it is thus difficult to envisage spot TC/RCs remaining at their current levels for anything other than a relatively short period of time. 

**Strong metal demand outlook in 2011 should bolster spot concentrate requirements** One potential shortcoming of the above analysis is that it focuses solely on the supply side of the equation without considering metal demand.  Under a weak cathode market scenario smelters might well opt to reduce operating rates to avoid competing in a low spot premia environment thereby suppressing incremental demand for concentrates.  However, we project a refined copper market deficit of ~500kt next year which will, no doubt, manifest itself in higher copper prices and spot premia (potentially more so with the imminent introduction of ETFs backed by physical copper).  Robust demand for refined copper and rising spot premia should heighten competition amongst smelters to satisfy consumer requirements, thereby bolstering demand for copper raw materials and in so doing suppress spot TC/RC terms.

In fact, the main disagreement amongst market commentators was on price outlook and in particular how hig

h the upside could be for the red metal.  To us, the next year or so certainly augurs well for the copper market, although at the same time we do detect a shift in the pace of mine project approvals as well as mine re-starts in marked contrast to the relative dearth of such developments during 2008 and 2009.  This shift has occurred in part due to confidence returning to the markets.  In addition, high prices have enabled many mining companies to re-build their balance sheets and they now have substantial cash reserves.  This creates a number of issues in itself, not least how to satisfy shareholders’ expectations of seeing this cash converted into further wealth-creating opportunities.  Many cash-rich companies also face the spectre of being takeover targets and are thus alert to the concept of “hunt or be hunted”.  At the same time the financial sector has become increasingly friendly towards lending money to copper mine projects which is also contributing to the accelerating pace of project approvals.  During 2010 various high profile projects have received board approval, including Aktogay (100kt/a), Antamina expansion (100kt/a), Antapaccay (160kt/a), Ernest Henry underground (110kt/a), Jabal Sayid (60kt/a), Konkola North (100kt/a), Las Bambas (400kt/a), Mirador (60kt/a) and Oyu Tolgoi (200kt/a initially).  Also, Freeport has re-started its Morenci mill (75kt/a Cu) and will reactivate its Chino mill (95kt/a) by 2012.  We have also heard that Southern Copper is readying its Cananea mine to be re-opened in mid-December and this will add almost 200kt/a to supplies when at full capacity.  The company is also studying expansion plans that would lift mill output by 190kt/a and SxEw production by 50kt/a.  Greenfield and brownfield mine developments are clearly crucial in offsetting attrition and closures of existing capacity and for satisfying incremental demand growth.  However, would-be developers should be mindful of the rapid increase in the number of projects that are now being approved for construction in the context of future metal demand (not forgetting China’s aspirations in securing metal units from its own offshore mine projects).  Last LME Week, for example, our numbers pointed to a supply gap relative to our base case mine production forecast of 3Mt/a by 2015, although in the space of just one year this gap has already closed by 1Mt/a.  Adding in highly probable projects to these base case forecasts the comparable numbers are 1.6Mt/a and 600kt/a, respectively.

**Collahuasi workers vote to strike** Workers at the Collahuasi mine in Chile voted overwhelmingly in favour of strike action after rejecting management’s latest pay offer.  The existing contract expired in late October and the company’s latest offer, which included an $18k “end of conflict” bonus, was turned down by 1415 union members with only seven voting in favour of the deal.  Under Chilean labour laws five days of mediated talks are allowed before a strike can begin. Last year the operation produced 493kt of copper-in-concentrates and 43kt of SxEw Cu.  This year’s forecast is similar assuming no disruptions due to industrial unrest. 

**Dexing mine expansion underway - targets 2012 start up** China’s Jiangxi Copper has started an expansion at its Dexing mine that will raise output by 41kt/a Cu at a cost of $43M.  The work is expected to be completed in 2012 at which time the open pit mining rate will be lifted by 30kt/d to 130kt/d.  Dexing is currently China’s largest copper mine with an existing capacity of 135kt/a Cu. 

**Freeport to re-start Chino** As mentioned, in its Q3 press release Freeport announced that it would re-start its Chino mill in New Mexico by 2012.
